Scientific theory of Earth's [[Lithosphere|lithosphere]] as divided into large tectonic plates that have been slowly moving since 3–4 billion years ago. It grew out of continental drift, proposed by [[Alfred Wegener]] in 1912, and was accepted after seafloor spreading was validated in the mid- to late 1960s.

The lithosphere, the rigid outer shell including the crust and upper mantle, is fractured into seven or eight major plates and many minor ones, riding on the ductile asthenosphere beneath. Relative motion defines three boundary types: convergent, divergent, and transform. Plates move from 10 to 40 mm a year at the [[Mid-Atlantic Ridge]] to about 160 mm a year for the Nazca plate. Boundaries are geologically active, with [[Earthquake|earthquakes]], volcanic activity, mountain-building, and [[Oceanic trench|oceanic trench]] formation; about 90% of earthquakes occur there. [[Hotspot (geology)|Hotspot]] volcanism produces volcanoes far from boundaries.

At convergent boundaries, subduction carries one plate's edge down under another into the mantle, reducing Earth's surface area. New oceanic crust formed at divergent margins by seafloor spreading balances the loss in a tectonic "conveyor belt." Density variations in the mantle produce [[Convection|convection]] currents, and the sinking of cold, dense oceanic crust at subduction zones is the strongest driver of plate motion; other proposed factors, such as tidal drag of the Moon, are debated.

Earth is the only planet known to have active plate tectonics. Jupiter's moon [[Europa (moon)|Europa]] shows signs of moving ice plates, and Mars and Venus are thought to have had tectonic activity in the past.

Ancient Greek philosopher of [[Classical Athens]], most commonly considered the foundational thinker of the Western philosophical tradition. Born into an aristocratic Athenian family, he descended through his mother from [[Solon]], credited with laying the foundations of Athenian democracy. He grew up during the [[Peloponnesian War]] and, according to ancient writers, wrote poetry until he met [[Socrates]] and turned to philosophy.

Socrates became his teacher and greatest source of inspiration. Plato never speaks in his own voice in his dialogues, and every dialogue except the *Laws* features Socrates; how far the Socrates of the dialogues reflects the historical man remains contested among scholars. The prosecution of Socrates by Anytus ended Plato's plans for a political career. He was influenced by Pythagoras, Heraclitus, and Parmenides.

Plato was an innovator of the literary dialogue and dialectic forms and influenced all the major areas of theoretical and practical philosophy. He founded the Academy, a school in Athens, around 387 BC, where he taught the body of philosophical theories later known as Platonism; his students included [[Aristotle]]. His most famous contribution is the [[Theory of forms|Theory of Forms]], which posits immutable ideal archetypes beyond the sensible world and aims to solve the problem of universals. In the [[Republic (Plato)|*Republic*]] he outlined an ideal state ruled by philosopher-kings; admirers have praised its rationalism, while critics have pointed to its censorship of the arts and rigid class structure as potentially authoritarian.

 His complete works are believed to have survived, unlike those of nearly all his contemporaries. [[Alfred North Whitehead]] said that "the safest general characterization of the European philosophical tradition is that it consists of a series of footnotes to Plato."

Range of intrinsically motivated activities done for recreation. Play is commonly associated with children but may occur at any life stage and among higher-functioning animals, most notably [[Mammal|mammals]] and [[Bird|birds]]. Though often seen as frivolous, it can be intensely focused, particularly when structured and goal-oriented, as in a [[Game|game]]; it ranges from spontaneous to planned or even compulsive.

Johan Huizinga's *Homo Ludens* (1944), the seminal text of play studies, defined play as a free activity standing consciously outside "ordinary" life, not serious yet absorbing the player intensely, connected with no material interest, and proceeding within its own boundaries of time and space according to fixed rules. This "magic circle" notion treats play as a separate sphere of human activity. [[Jean Piaget]] remarked that the many theories of play prove the phenomenon difficult to understand. The National Playing Fields Association defines it as freely chosen, personally directed, intrinsically motivated behavior that actively engages the child.

Play takes the forms of improvisation, pretense, mimicry, games, [[Sport|sports]], and thrill-seeking. Roger Caillois, in *Man, Play and Games* (1961), interpreted many social structures as elaborate forms of games. Free-form play lets children change the rules at will; structured play has defined goals and rules. Designed spaces include sports fields and [[Playground|playgrounds]]. The National Institute for Play describes seven patterns, including attunement, body, creative, object, social, and storytelling play. Another scheme distinguishes challenge play, such as solving a [[Rubik's Cube]], from competitive, construction, cooperative, nurturing, and replica play.

Evolutionary accounts hold that play rehearses skills such as motor coordination and conflict resolution. Researchers report that unstructured play improves impulse control, language, and empathy in children.

Inflammatory condition of the [[Lung|lung]] primarily affecting the alveoli, the small air sacs. Symptoms typically include some combination of productive or dry cough, chest pain, fever, and difficulty breathing; in elderly people confusion may be the most prominent sign. Severity varies.

It is usually caused by infection with viruses or bacteria, and less commonly by fungi and parasites. Common causes include *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, [[Influenza|influenza]] viruses, and [[Respiratory syncytial virus]]; in about half of cases no causative agent is isolated. It is classified by where it was acquired: community-acquired, hospital-acquired, or healthcare-associated. Risk factors include smoking, immunodeficiency, alcoholism, [[Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease]], [[Sickle cell disease]], asthma, diabetes, and heart failure. In children, additional risks include not being breastfed, malnutrition, and poverty.

Diagnosis is often based on symptoms and physical examination; chest X-rays, blood tests, and sputum culture may help confirm it. Treatment depends on the cause. Pneumonia believed to be bacterial is treated with [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]], such as [[Amoxicillin|amoxicillin]]; oxygen therapy may be used if oxygen levels are low, and severe cases generally require hospitalization. Prevention includes [[Vaccine|vaccines]] against certain causes, hand washing, and not smoking.

Each year pneumonia affects about 450 million people globally (7% of the population) and causes about 4 million deaths. Survival has greatly improved since antibiotics and vaccines were introduced in the 20th century, but the disease remains a leading cause of death in developing countries and among the very old, the very young, and the chronically ill.

Form of literary art that uses aesthetic and often rhythmic qualities of language to evoke meanings in addition to, or in place of, literal ones. The word comes from the Greek *poiesis*, "making." Poets use devices such as assonance, alliteration, onomatopoeia, rhythm (via metre), and rhyme schemes to produce musical or other artistic effects, and organize them into structures that may be strict or loose, conventional or invented. Most written poems are set in verse, a series of lines that follow the poetic structure.

Not all traditions depend on rhyme and regular meter: Biblical poetry and alliterative verse use other means, and Somali poetry relies on complex systems of alliteration and metre independent of writing. Much modern poetry forgoes rhyme or set rhythm. Ambiguity, symbolism, and figures of speech such as metaphor and metonymy often leave a poem open to multiple interpretations.

Some scholars believe poetry predates literacy and developed from folk epics and oral genres; others suggest it did not necessarily predate writing. The oldest surviving epic poem, the [[Epic of Gilgamesh]], dates from the 3rd millennium BC in [[Sumer]]. The Egyptian *Story of Sinuhe* dates to c. 1800 BC, and the Pyramid Texts of the 25th century BC are among the earliest written poetry in Africa. Other early poems include the Chinese *Shijing*, the Sanskrit *Rigveda*, the Hebrew Psalms, the [[Iliad]] and the [[Odyssey]], Virgil's [[Aeneid]], and the Indian [[Ramayana]] and [[Mahabharata]]. [[Aristotle]]'s *Poetics* analyzed poetry within the uses of speech in rhetoric, drama, song, and comedy.

Country in Central Europe, with over 37 million people; capital and largest city [[Warsaw]]. Officially the Republic of Poland, it extends from the [[Baltic Sea]] in the north to the Sudetes and Carpathian Mountains in the south and covers 312,696 sq km. It borders Lithuania and Russia to the northeast, Belarus and Ukraine to the east, Slovakia and the Czech Republic to the south, and Germany to the west. It has sixteen voivodeships; other major cities include Kraków, Wrocław, Łódź, Poznań, Gdańsk, and Szczecin.

The West Slavic Polans gave the country its name. A Polan ruler, [[Mieszko I]], converted to Christianity in 966, and the Kingdom of Poland emerged in 1025. In 1569 the union with Lithuania formed the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]], a great power with an elective monarchy that adopted Europe's first modern constitution in 1791. Russia, Prussia, and Austria partitioned the country at the end of the 18th century, and independence returned in 1918.

In September 1939 the [[Invasion of Poland|invasion]] by Germany and the Soviet Union began World War II, which brought [[The Holocaust|the Holocaust]] and millions of Polish casualties. Poland then entered the Eastern Bloc and signed the Warsaw Pact. The Solidarity movement, which emerged in 1980, helped initiate the fall of the Iron Curtain; the communist government was dissolved and free elections were held in 1989.

Poland is a republic with a bicameral legislature of the Sejm and the Senate. It is a high-income developed country, the 21st largest economy by nominal GDP and the sixth in the European Union. It has 18 UNESCO World Heritage Sites and 23 national parks. A founding member of the United Nations, it joined [[NATO]] in 1999 and the [[European Union]] in 2004.

Constituted body of people empowered by a state to enforce the law and protect public order and the public itself. Police powers encompass arrest and the use of force legitimized by the [[State (polity)|state's]] monopoly on violence. Forces are usually public-sector services funded through taxes and are often defined as separate from the [[Military|military]], although the [[Gendarmerie|gendarmerie]] are military units charged with civil policing. Core functions include preventing and detecting crime, maintaining order, investigating offenses, controlling traffic, and responding to emergencies.

The word entered English in the early 15th century from Middle French *police* ("public order, administration, government"), from Latin *politia* and Greek *politeia*. [[Ireland]] uses the terms Garda and Gardaí for its national force and its members.

According to [[Michel Foucault]], the modern concept of police as a paid functionary of the state was developed by German and French legal scholars in the 17th and early 18th centuries, notably in Nicolas Delamare's *Traité de la Police* (1705). Under the German *Polizeiwissenschaft*, police duties extended to public health, urban planning, and the surveillance of prices. Preventive policing gained influence in the late 18th century; [[Jeremy Bentham]] promoted the view of [[Cesare Beccaria]] that preventing crimes is better than punishing them. London's Metropolitan Police, established in 1829, became a model for modern organized policing.

In some societies in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, police developed to maintain the class system and protect private property. Their role remains controversial: they may be involved to varying degrees in corruption, brutality, and the enforcement of authoritarian rule, and debates over accountability, use of force, and the balance between security and civil liberties continue.

Organization that coordinates candidates to compete in elections and participate in governance. Members commonly hold similar ideas about politics, and parties may promote specific ideological or policy goals. Parties are a major part of the politics of almost every country; most countries have several, while others have one. They matter in autocracies, which often have a single governing party, as well as in [[Democracy|democracies]], and some political scientists consider competition between parties essential to democracy.

A party usually includes a leader, executives who handle administration, and members who may volunteer, donate, and vote for its candidates. Parties may cooperate closely with affiliated organizations such as a [[Trade union|trade union]], a youth organization, or an armed wing. They differ from parliamentary groups, internal factions, and advocacy groups chiefly in focusing on electing candidates, and tend to have larger membership and a deeper connection to the [[Election|electorate]].

Many parties are driven by ideology: liberal, conservative, and socialist parties are common in democratic elections, as are [[Communism|communist]], [[Populism|populist]], nationalist, and Islamist ones. Others have no ideology and engage mainly in patronage or clientelism, or are "big tent" parties seeking voters with varied positions.

Factions are ancient; the late Roman Republic had the Populares and Optimates. Scholars differ on when modern parties emerged. Some point to 17th-century Britain after the [[Glorious Revolution]], when the Whigs backed Protestant constitutional monarchy against absolute rule; others place the rise of mass-based parties in the 1820s–1840s. The [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]] of the United Kingdom and the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] of the United States are both frequently called the world's oldest continuous party. Critics, including James Madison, have warned that factionalism exacerbates social divisions, while defenders credit parties with aggregating interests into coherent platforms.

Academic discipline that studies politics, systems of governance and power, political behavior and thought, and associated constitutions and laws. Unlike [[Political philosophy|political philosophy]], which is primarily normative and judges politics by values, it emphasizes descriptive and explanatory accounts and favors empirical evidence over ethical judgments.

The field emerged as a distinct discipline in the late 19th century, influenced by [[Empiricism|empiricism]] and [[Positivism|positivism]], from history, philosophy, and law amid the professionalization of universities. *Political Science Quarterly* was established in 1886, and its first issue defined political science as "the science of the state." The American Political Science Association (APSA) was founded in 1903 and the *American Political Science Review* in 1906; APSA now serves more than 11,000 members in more than 100 countries. A UNESCO initiative led to the International Political Science Association in 1949, with national associations in France in 1949, Britain in 1950, and West Germany in 1951.

The behavioral revolution of the 1950s shifted emphasis to explaining human behavior from a neutral point of view using [[Quantitative research|quantitative methods]] such as surveys and empirical testing. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, [[Game theory|game-theoretic]] modeling borrowed from economics was applied to institutions such as the U.S. Congress and to voting, led by William H. Riker and colleagues at the University of Rochester. The Perestroika Movement of 2000 reacted against what its supporters called the "mathematicization" of the field and argued for a plurality of methodologies.

Its main subfields are political theory, comparative politics, [[International relations|international relations]], American politics, political methodology, and [[Public administration|public administration]]. Critics have raised concerns about the field's replicability and about the political leanings of its practitioners.

Activity of settling affairs in an organized society, usually by resolving issues through a [[Government|government]]. People engaged in it are politicians, and the branch of social science that studies politics and government is [[Political science|political science]]. Methods include promoting one's views among people, negotiating, making laws, and exercising internal and external force, including warfare against adversaries. Politics operates at levels from clans and tribes of traditional societies through local governments, companies, and institutions to sovereign states and the international level. In modern states people often form parties to represent their ideas, and an election is usually a competition between parties. A political system is a framework that defines acceptable political methods within a society. The word may be used positively, as in a compromising and non-violent "political solution," or descriptively, as "the art or science of government," but it often carries a negative connotation.

The English word derives from Greek *polis*, "city." Aristotle's *Politiká* ("affairs of the cities") was rendered in the mid-15th century as *Polettiques*, which became Politics; the singular *politic* is attested in English from 1430.

Writers differ on what counts as political. Adrian Leftwich distinguished an extensive view, which finds politics across all human social relations, from a limited view that restricts it to certain contexts such as governance. The feminist slogan "the personal is political" belongs to the extensive view. Robert A. Dahl argued that politics may be defined by the use of power. Political moralists link politics closely to ethics; [[Hannah Arendt]] wrote that for Aristotle, being political meant that everything was decided through words and persuasion rather than violence. Realists, a group that some scholars say includes [[Niccolò Machiavelli]], [[Thomas Hobbes]], and Harold Lasswell, see its true nature in the human desire for rule and self-interest; Lasswell defined it as determining "who gets what, when, and how." Elmer Schattschneider held that conflict lies at the root of all politics, and Carl Schmitt saw its essence in distinguishing friend from foe, while Aristotle and Bernard Crick took more cooperative views. Michael Laver described it as a blend of conflict and co-operation.

Early bands and tribes lacked centralized political structures. Theories of early state formation include voluntary theories, which stress shared rational interest and the pressures that followed the development of agriculture, including the hydraulic hypothesis tying the state to large-scale irrigation; and conflict theories, which stress dominance of one group over others and warfare. The first states were early dynastic [[Sumer]] and early dynastic Egypt, which arose around 3000 BC. Egyptians, Romans, and Greeks were the first known to formulate a political philosophy of the state and analyze political institutions rationally; before that, states were justified through religious myths. The history of political thought reaches back to early antiquity, with seminal works such as [[Plato]]'s *Republic*, Aristotle's *Politics*, Confucius's political manuscripts, and Chanakya's *Arthashastra*. Greek city-states and the Roman Republic produced key innovations, including direct democracy in Athens, where citizenship was combined with directly democratic government.
